speechtext:
-who has revealed in his quiet and thoughtful way a grasp of the economics of this country which has far exceeded that of people opposite. If any savant in the party supporting the government wants to know why public opinion polls are showing greater and greater support for this party, it is because month after month people are appreciating the economic wisdom of the Leader of the Opposition. I will give the government that diagnosis for free. If they are thoughtful, they will note his suggestions for our economy which preceded the turnabout of the former finance minister. They will note, too, how perceptively he has analyzed the economic situation. Many of the better moves of the present minister, and in his latter days of his predecessor, were made when they picked up some of the suggestions of the Leader of the Opposition. In his very fine speech during the budget debate, he presented two further important suggestions which I think will find favour among Canadians and have an important effect upon the national economy.
To take satisfaction out of the state of Canada's economic affairs today is surely an exercise in myopic nonobservation. How can we strut about and say how well off we are, how beautifully things are going, when unemployment stalks the land year after year? In the old days of classic economic teachings, we were told that these two things came in sequence; inflation might follow unemployment. But the present government has mastered the art of bringing them on simultaneously and continuously, seemingly with no prospect of making either one of them
May 23, 1972

disappear. There is far too much poverty in the just society, too much inequality among Canadian people and among the regions of Canada.
I happen to come from a region which knows the pangs and inequity of regional disparity. The province of Prince Edward Island, so richly blessed in many ways, is today in the unenviable position of having the highest unemployment rate of all the provinces. We have even surpassed Newfoundland. The figure for March was 16.2 per cent, and combined with this, figures on the cost of living which I have just received today, show that the index in the City of Charlottetown, taking January, 1969 as a base of 100, stands, in April of 1972, at 114.5. Compare that with the figure for another area, St. John the home of my whip, known for its high cost of living-109.8-and 106.7 for the other Atlantic centre, the city of Halifax. So we have the effects of both inflation and unemployment, uniquely painful to the people who must endure them simultaneously. In these circumstances I find it very difficult to tell the people of Prince Edward Island or the people of the Atlantic region they have never had it so good. Ask the young people of Canada how things are going today? Ask the graduates who are coming out of our fine universities by thousands and thousands. Ask them if the economy is going well. I talked to a young student the other day. I said: "Have you applied to the Canada Manpower office for a job?" He said: "Are you kidding? I have been there 45 times."
Much was made by some speakers this afternoon of various programs, including Opportunities for Youth, and the LIP program. They offer something, of course, and with our statistics so high in the realm of unemployment, of course we welcome them. But what happens when the six or seven weeks are over? What happens when the $38,000 or $58,000 or $78,000 is spent and the 12, 13 or 15 jobs peter out at the end of the project? These are mere palliatives. They are not nearly enough for the hundreds of thousands of Canadian people, especially the young who are crying out for opportunities. We all know very well that the projects which are accepted are far outnumbered by other projects, probably of real value and virtue, which are rejected.
We have had discussions in this House during this debate on the general question of regional disparity. A hard and dispassionate look at the statistics-though it is difficult for me to be dispassionate-indicates that the gap is not narrowing. By many important economic indices it is broadening; getting worse. Yet we have a situation where practically the whole country is a designated area. I suppose this is part of the reason that when practically the whole of the generality becomes the special, there is nothing very special left, because almost everything becomes a designated area.
I was much interested in the intervention of my hon. and learned friend the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) who was euphoric almost to the point of excitement over this budget. He thought it was one of the greatest that had ever come along. On May 15, as reported at page 2259 of Hansard, he said:
The Budget-Mr. Macquarrie
According to those who are in a position to judge, Canada has a record second to none throughout the world in recent years in terms of the expansion of the economy and the control of inflation.
So, mention was made of controlling inflation. Another modest outburst came a few paragraphs later when he said:
In the last three or four years, we have achieved a record that is second to none in the history of this country.
He then designated the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) as having worked well abroad on behalf of Canadian industry, though earlier he had said that if Oscars were given out for economic performance Canada would have been one of the recipients. He might not have been so timid and suggested that we should have had them all. In other words, whatever proposals were made by the minister would not be designated, as were Swift's, as modest proposals.
I thought it interesting that the Secretary of State for External Affairs should intervene so strongly on behalf of his colleague the Minister of Finance. Then, I reflected upon it a bit and came to the conclusion that it was not so strange really because it is in fact in the external world that some of our great problems have arisen. Things are happening there that are injuring our domestic economy. One of the areas where I have quarreled consistently and differed continuously with the present government is with regard to their white paper projection of a foreign policy for Canadians. Hon. members will recall the following paragraph on "Foreign policy in essence":
In undertaking this review the Government has been constantly reminded of its need and responsibility to choose carefully aims, objectives and priorities in sufficiently long and broad terms to ensure that essential Canadian interests and values are safeguarded in the world situation where rapid and even radical changes can be anticipated as normal rather than exceptional conditions. Canada, like other states, must act accordingly to how it perceives its aims and interest. External activities should be directly related to national policies pursued within Canada, and serve the same objectives. Diplomatic relations are maintained and strengthened for a wide variety of reasons-among others, trade expansion, collective security, cultural contact, co-operation in development assistance, exchanges in science and technology.
Such relationships have to be kept under review to ensure that they continue to serve Canada's objectives effectively. Those may change as both Canada and the world change. In essence, foreign policy is the product of the Government's progressive definition and pursuit of national aims and interests in the international environment. It is the extension abroad of national policies.
I think it is not. I think foreign policy is much more than that. As a decent, responsible and well-endowed member of the international community, we should think of foreign policy as much more than an extension of our domestic situation.
Also raised in this debate is the opposite issue, the effect of external movements and non-movements on the domestic situation. External developments and decisions have affected, and affected unhelpfully, our domestic economy. I believe that this is one of the serious weaknesses affecting our economy today. When we do have a foreign policy debate I should like to discuss the "neo-Mackenzie Kin-gism" which pervades our foreign policy, but I am more concerned today at the statement made by the deputy minister of trade in Czechoslavakia that Canada could be
2474

May 23, 1972
The Budget-Mr. Macquarrie selling more goods there except for the fact that Canada itself is dragging its feet.
On May 3 a very interesting compilation of statistics by Statistics Canada was issued on March trade. According to a report in the Ottawa Citizen of that date:
Exports during March this year totalled $1,501 billion, barely above the $1,498 billion figure for March, 1971, Statistics Canada reports.
The slight increase was the result of increased exports to the U.S. and declines in exports to almost all other countries.
Exports to the U.S. rose to $1,119 billion from $1,041 billion-
The statistics indicated a trend to increased Canadian dependence on the U.S. market is continuing, despite federal government efforts to open up other foreign markets. Exports to Britain were $8.6 million for March, down from $90.9 million a year earlier.
Other declines: Japan, down to $55.4 million from $75.8 million; West Germany, down to $17.6 million from $26.9 million; Norway, down to $18.3 million from $24.3 million; Italy, down to $14.9 million from $20.8 million; Australia, down to $12.7 million from $22.5 million; Venezuela, down to $8.7 million from $20.1 million; Belgium-Luxemburg, down to $5.9 million from $12.4 million; and India, down to $5.1 million from $9.7 million.
This is a dreary threnody of trade declines to the very kind of country to which our export trade should be booming. Exports of newsprint fell, as did exports of aluminum, copper and automobiles. Is this the kind of record, Mr. Speaker, that is second to none, with an increasing dependence upon the United States market and a continual slipping in other very important markets? Instead of patting ourselves on the back for how well we are doing, I think we should and must make vigorous efforts to stimulate trade all across the world today, and to diversify our trade.
I was amused-though I am sure this was not meant unkindly-by the denigration that the Secretary of State for External Affairs made of the former minister of trade and commerce in the government that I supported. This hon. gentleman was known as a great and aggressive promoter of Canadian trade, and he has been constantly needling and nagging the present government to expand our trade in the markets of the world. Why do we not have more trade offices if this is what is needed? Can we not negotiate with those on each side of the Iron Curtain for more trade offices? If we have to do a better job of selling our goods, then what is holding us back? This is part of this withdrawal syndrome. There are ten countries in the world that have full-fledged ambassadors and embassies in Ottawa to which we have yet to appoint any ambassador. We have not reciprocated the representation.
We have not even yet got around to appointing a High Commissioner to Barbados, a country of 200,000 people which for several years has had a three-member high commission in this city. We have not appointed an ambassador solely accredited to the European Common Market, and if there is any economy or political aggregation more important on today's horizon than that vast united Europe which is developing with the admission of the United Kingdom and other countries, I do not know what it would be. Is this government aware of what is taking place? As I say, Sir, we have not got around to doing what many other countries have done, appointing an ambassador in Brussels solely accredited to that vast and growing aggregation.

Let me read from a very modern and able economist, Dian Cohen, writing in the Toronto Star in respect of the admission of the United Kingdom to the European Common Market. She says:
What is possibly more significant in the long run is that Canada is increasingly being left out in the cold by a world which is aligning itself into massive trading blocs. We are rapidly reaching the point where our only role in the world economy will be to react to external events.
Then, what will we tell the producers of Canada? Will we say then that they have never had it so good? We are in danger of being left out and losing our trade capacity with many of the countries forming the EEC, as well as others out of it. Should we not be concerned and troubled?
Many of my colleagues have dealt with our relations with the United States. Many have described how the government has blown an uncertain trumpet, lo these many months. Do the people of Canada know what is going to happen with the TAPS route? Do they really know what is going to happen about the Mackenzie route? Do they really know how much our government has studied either one of them, and do they really know how forthrightly, clearly and consistently our government has conveyed its views to the United States on either one of them? Is it too fearsome a prophecy to suggest that the people of Canada, if they do not watch out, will end up with both routes and have the invidious dangers to the environment from both of them, not just one? Are they given clear information on this?
Have the people of Canada been told where we stand and where we do not stand on the growing European community? Do they know what we are doing about the possibilities of trade with that area? Do they know what has been done about the market we once had with the United Kingdom? Has the government been alert to the dangers of a rapidly changing world economy?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am glad there is someone who is satisfied. Speaking of uncertain trumpets, I just heard one.
I would look at another area of great concern, and I see my colleague, the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) is here. He is an expert in this field. What are we doing to protect the industry which today is probably in more deadly peril than any other, and that is the historic fishing industry? This is a prime industry of this country, and the situation is hurtful to the whole industry and hurtful to the whole of Canada. We have made great proclamations and talked about a 12-mile limit. No one gets in there; no Australian ships are allowed in there, and no Swiss ships are allowed in there. Of course, they do not come anyway, but those that do come have historic rights which they still hold. We have seemingly made no effort, diplomatically or otherwise, to oust those who are bringing depradation to the great resources of the sea off the east coast and off the west coast as well. In the face of the problem with the Danish government in reference to salmon, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) screwed up his courage and suggested a personal boycott,
May 23, 1972

but it was clearly ordained the day after that it was a mere personal boycott.
Have we successfully asserted our claims to fisheries management over the continental shelf? There are so many issues that cause thoughtful people great anxiety I am convinced that it is the mismanagement of things abroad which has been one of the large contributors to the ills of our economy at home. We are missing the boat in trade; we are withdrawing from those areas of world activity where we should be functioning at a high pitch with intensive involvement; we are failing to be vigorous in markets of the world and, as I documented a few minutes ago, we are losing markets which are precious and valuable to us. These are the kinds of things which must be considered not only in this debate, but which must be and will be considered by the Canadian people. It is that consideration and that kind of forecast of what conditions should be that is no doubt the reason we are still here and not out on the hustings testing the wind of public opinion on the economic mismanagement of this government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I deem it a privilege to participate in this debate at this particular point, following the speech we have just heard by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie). To start off my speech this afternoon, I should like to give him an example of the great economic savings and advantages which are the record of his present leader, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) in this House of Commons. Let me quote from a report of a meeting of the Standing Committee of this House of Commons on National Resources and Public Works when the Atomic Energy of Canada officials appeared before it a couple of weeks ago. At that time the chairman asked the following question of Mr. Gray, President of Atomic Energy of Canada, Limited:
As you know, we are purchasing heavy water from as many areas in the world as we can. Can you give us the names of those countries and the costs that we are paying per pound for that heavy water at the present time? By comparison, what would heavy water cost us if we were in a position to produce enough to service ourselves as a nation?
To this question Mr. Gray replied:
We have bought a lot from the United States at varying prices starting at $24 a pound, going to $28 a pound, going to $30 a pound, and they have just announced that the price is now $39 a pound. We bought some from Sweden at $31; we bought some from Russia at two prices, $30 and I think the last was around $32 a pound; and we bought some from Britain at $30 a pound. We have leased some from Argentina at a 7 per cent charge, which we have to send back.
Had Glace Bay-
This is the plant which was originated by the hon. Leader of the Opposition in this House when he was Premier of Nova Scotia. Quoting again:
Had Glace Bay produced heavy water, as it was supposed to do, we would be in a surplus position and would not have had to buy any of this expensive heavy water. This runs into quite a few millions because their contract price started at $20.50 a pound and dropped down to $16 a pound, for an average of $18.15. That is the same number for the Canadian General Electric existing contract. At the moment we have been buying their production at $20.50 a pound. So you can see that there is a big mark-up between $20 and the new price of $39. I suppose we have averaged $30 a pound over all this production, which is something like 1,600 tons. We have
25316-33J
The Budget-Mr. Hopkins
paid at least $10 more a pound, which comes to around $30 million extra.
Is this the type of economy or the kind of economic measures the opposition in this House of Commons would offer to the Canadian people at a time when this government has the best record in many fields of any nation in the western world today?
Let us start looking at some of the positive things in life. We live in a nation which has the greatest potential. I believe the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Murphy) was correct when he asked whether, because with all the faults at our own doorstep, we ever compared our economy and problems with those of other nations in the world. I have asked this question in this House before, and I ask it again. Who would exchange his way of life in Canada today for that of a person in any other nation in the world? Let us stand up, be counted, and go ahead with a positive attitude for the development of this country. I say on behalf of all members of this House of Commons if some of the backbenchers in this House of Commons were listened to once in a while, those who have firsthand knowledge of their constituencies, and if their recommendations were taken to heart and proper measures followed, we would not have some of the problems which exist today at all levels of government.
I shall give a positive example of this. I do not pretend to be a prophet, but on October 22, 1970 in a speech in this House of Commons as recorded at page 475 of Hansard I stated the following:
I want to say a few words about transportation. It is my view that equitable freight rates and good roads are important in developing the Canadian economy, as are our very worth-while policies of regional economic expansion.
I wish to say at this stage that I am not a critic of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. I remember the days in 1962 when there were nearly 3,000 people in the unemployment rolls in the city of Pembroke at a time when members of the official opposition were in power. Not one single effort was made to alleviate the unemployment situation in that area at that time. I give the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Mar-chand) full marks for at least having the gumption and intestinal fortitude to stand up, be counted, and produce a program whether or not he may be criticized for the administration of it. It is only the doers in this world who are criticized and not the armchair critics.
In that same speech of October 22, 1970,1 also stated:
We in the Ottawa valley have always been plagued with unsatisfactory road conditions. If there is one thing we badly need, it is a good highway artery.
Let me give the House a good example of what I mean. The bridge in the centre of the town of Petawawa that spans the Petawawa River was built before the first troops moved into Base Petawawa in 1907. Today, it is called upon to handle all the traffic moving into Base Petawawa from various parts of the country, as well as traffic destined for Chalk River. Invariably there is a big traffic jam right in the middle of the town of Petawawa during the rush hour, and it is nothing for cars to be lined up for three miles. One morning about two weeks ago the nuclear laboratories at Chalk River lost $2,000 in wages which the Crown Corporation had to absorb because employees were late through no fault of their own. Renfrew County Council has brought this problem to the attention of the Minister of Highways of Ontario. It sent a

May 23, 1972
The Budget-Mr. Hopkins
resolution to the Minister of Highways of Ontario requesting the early completion of the proposed highway 417. The hon. member for Lanark-Renfew-Carleton (Mr. McBride) and myself were asked to support this brief, and we did so.
In reply to my letter to the Minister of Highways, the Hon. George E. Gomme, I was informed that roads were not the only problems in eastern Ontario, and that if we had really wanted to admit it, another problem was lack of economic development policies. He suggested that if the hon. member for Lanark-Ren-frew-Carleton and myself had succeeded in getting the area designated, this would have gone a long way toward solving our problems. In other words, the minister was trying to pass the buck to us. Let me tell the Hon. George Gomme that the hon. members for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton and Renfrew North have now done their homework and we are looking for him to do his.
I delivered that speech shortly after the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton and I had succeeded, through speeches in this House, and through talking to party officials, in convincing our ministers in this House of Commons that the Ottawa River valley is very important, very much like parts of the Maritimes. It is also very closely related to the Maritimes. A number of us who have relatives in these areas travel back and forth. We were able to convince the ministers concerned that this area required economic policies. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion saw fit to declare our area a special area under regional economic expansion. We have reaped some benefits from that program.
Let me tell you, however, what has happened since then with regard to Mr. Gomme's statement to me that another problem must be met which was related to economic development. I stated we had done our homework on this subject. Mr. Gomme, as Minister of Highways and his successor, the new Minister of Transportation and Communications, as late as January 28, 1972 advised the then Minister of National Defence that no second bridge was required across the Petawawa River because a start was to be made on highway 417. Shortly after that, an announcement was made that construction would start in 1973. Originally, the starting date was 1975. I can only say that in 1869 the Canadian government bought the Hudson's Bay Company land in western Canada in order to build a railway across this nation. Without the technological knowledge we have in this modern age, the Canadian engineers of that day built the Canadian Pacific Railway across this nation and had it completed by 1885. We have such a progressive Department of Highways, Transportation and Communications in Ontario today that it takes several years to build a very important bridge across the Petawawa River.
At midnight of May 6, the present bridge collapsed, the very bridge about which I spoke in this House two years ago. At that time, I wrote a letter of complaint to the highways minister of the province of Ontario and received an arrogant answer from him. When the bridge collapsed, several families were stranded on the north side, the site of the Canadian forces base, Petawawa. In order to get the military personnel to assist the civilian authorities, the request must come from the province concerned. I made six or seven telephone calls to Queens Park, Toronto, to try to locate a provincial minister, but I could not even get an answer from the switchboard at Queens Park, Toronto. I even made a phone call to

Ottawa to try to locate a provincial minister. Is this the kind of progressive government that this great new Colgate premier of the province of Ontario is giving us today?
On Sunday, May 7 I sent a telex to the premier of Ontario requesting that a state of crisis be declared and that emergency measures be taken to assist in dealing with this problem because about 4,000 employees cross the bridge daily to and from work. My telex was backed by one from the warden of Renfrew County who is head of some 40 reeves across the county. It was also backed by a telex from the mayor of the city of Pembroke, one from the mayor of the town of Deep River and one from the reeves of Petawawa township and the village of Petawawa in which the military base is located. As of today, May 23, the premier of the province has not even had the courtesy to acknowledge a single one of those telexes from the elected officials in the area. I do not care what the premier of the province thinks of me as a person, but I respect his office and I expect him to respect what I represent, even if he cannot respect me personally. I also expect him to respect the office of the warden of Renfrew County, of the mayor of the city of Pembroke and the mayor of the town of Deep River. That is the least we can expect.
The old ball game has started once again. People have started asking, for what are we paying the Canadian armed forces? The bridge collapsed 450 feet away from the gateway to the second largest military base in Canada. First of all, let me point out that this bridge is part of a provincial highway and it is not the responsibility of the Department of National Defence in any way. They cannot take action until they are requested to do so by the province of Ontario which must take full legal responsibility for any action taken after the collapse of the bridge. The armed forces did not receive a request from the province of Ontario until the Friday following the collapse. Finally, the engineers checked the site toward the end of the week. The approaches to the river banks were built by the province, the abutments were put in by the province and the province took full legal responsibility for that action. I want to pay a compliment to the Canadian armed forces because General Quinn, commanding officer at base Petawawa, his staff and his military personnel have cooperated fully, and had it not been for them I do not know what we would have done. They followed the correct procedures.
Yesterday, 150 engineers from the Royal Canadian armed forces were on duty all day constructing a Bailey bridge. They started at eight this morning and at four p.m. they had 70 feet of the 260 foot span built. This shows the expertise of our ^rmed forces, and it shows what they can do when they are asked to do it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not want to hear it said that our armed forces today are not a professional group.
In the time that I have left, I should like to make a few remarks about an interprovincial national park that will make a great contribution towards achieving greater unity in this nation. We in the northern part of my constituency, in the area to the north of the Mattawa River and
May 23, 1972

on the Quebec side of the Ottawa River in the county of Temiscamingue, are working closely together to create the first interprovincial national park in Canada which would include areas on both sides of the Ottawa River. We are doing this not only as an example of unity between the two major provinces in central Canada, but because we know that people from all the urban areas of southern Canada, from Ontario, Quebec and the other provinces, will go into the national park when it is finished, will be travelling and talking together and thus will get to know one another.
The right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) is a great admirer of Sir John A. Macdonald. I, too, have read a great deal about him. He was a great asset to this country because of his flexibility in the early days of Canadian history. You will all remember that in 1864 he made his famous speech in Charlottetown in which he said-and I will not quote his exact words-that if you fellows and we fellows could get together once in a while and talk things over, we would learn what a wonderful person each one of us is. We want people from all areas of Quebec, as well as ethnic groups, to come to that interprovincial national park because they will share common interests. We want them to socialize in the restaurants and recreation complexes that will surround the national park and to get to know each other.
This will do far more for the unity of the nation than the political confrontations and the uprisings and disturbances that have taken place lately. We have to take positive steps toward this goal. It was with that thought in mind that I introduced two private members bills for first reading in the House a few days ago. It was rather interesting to hear the comments that have been made following the introduction of the bills. First of all, I am sick and tired of seeing the symbols of various countries abused, specifically the flags representing those nations. I recommend in these bills, and I will recommend on any platform, that the tearing down, the burning and the desecrating of the Canadian or of provincial flags be made a criminal offence, and I recommend the same thing with regard to the flag of any foreign nation lawfully represented in Canada.
I would like to recount an anecdote which appeared in the Canadian Press. I refer to an article in the Globe and Mail of May 2 which reads as follows:
Under two private bills introduced in the Commons yesterday it would be illegal to deface the official flags of Canada and even the U.S. Stars and Stripes or China's Red Flag.
The bills, introduced by Leonard Hopkins (L, Renfrew North) would make it an offence to harm the flags of Canada or the provinces and of those countries whose governments "are legally represented in Canada."
Anybody who "destroys, disfigures, mutilates, defaces, defiles, desecrates or casts contempt upon the Canadian or provincial (or the prescribed foreign) flags is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction," the act says.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that it does become an act. There is an interesting anecdote to this. You know that we have some famous open line programs on our radio stations. It is amazing to hear the intelligent remarks made on some of these programs. I understand that one interesting commentator on a Kingston radio station picked up my bills
The Budget-Mr. Hopkins
and started a great discussion about who is this guy running around protecting communist flags? What is he doing all this for? Apparently I was the subject of heated debate in the whole Kingston area. Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this kind of publicity. There are some politicians who say that publicity is good for you, whether it is bad or good. I do not entirely agree with the former, but in any case this gives me a chance to speak on the Kingston radio station in an area where I am partially known, being a graduate of Queen's University, one of the fine old institutions in this country. I will be very interested to meet this intelligent commentator. Having taught school for 12 J years and having handled every grade from one to 13, I am not sure in which category this commentator falls. However, it will be interesting for me to make a clarifying statement when I am there, and I shall quote from my bills with great delight.
In all sincerity, Mr. Speaker, I would like to have from this House, and particularly from the front benches of my own party, the strongest possible support for the interprovincial national park that we are trying to create between Timiskaming and that great district of Nipissing. This is part of the area that was represented by the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Legault) before he gave it over to me, and what a lovely gift it was! While I am on this subject, Mr. Speaker, on a personal level may I say that it has been a great pleasure indeed to have such a fine gentleman and co-operative colleague to the north of me. He will be retiring from parliament at the end of this session, and I wish him every success in all his endeavours thereafter.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Ottawa River, Mr. Speaker, will run right through the middle of our proposed national park. I am sure the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Lefebvre), in view of the experience he has had in this regard during the last few days, will agree with me when I say that according to statistics 3 per cent of the logs that have been floated down the Ottawa River and its tributaries over the last 125 years are still lying in the Ottawa River. Statistics also indicate that an average of 5 per cent of the logs floated down these rivers by lumbering companies during the past ten years are still at the bottom of the Ottawa River. I received representations from groups who were interested in cleaning up the Ottawa river. A pilot project was launched last summer and one group formed a company. They took out a couple of thousand of these logs. Some were 50 years old, and they piled them up on the shores.
Shortly thereafter they were moved to a sawmill and the lumber products and by-products produced were of a high calibre and quite merchantable. This group has been offered, free of charge, all the logs lying in the Ottawa River owned by the companies that floated them down the Ottawa and its tributaries over the years. This group is now the Upper Ottawa Improvement Company, and it is made up of all the companies that have ever driven logs on the Ottawa River. To give credit to the Ontario government, Mr. Speaker, it has cancelled the timber dues that would normally be payable on delivery of these logs. Here we have the Upper Ottawa Improvement Company, made up of all these other companies, willing to donate all these logs lying between Ottawa and Lake Timiskaming. The

May 23, 1972
The Budget-Mr. Hopkins
company has the expertise to do the job. It could employ 200 men. It could feed sawmills on both the Quebec and Ontario sides of the river and create employment. We have many people who are capable of undertaking this type of employment because logging has been a long time tradition in the Ottawa Valley. However, it costs more than $4 per log to put each log out on the river shore.
We have gone to several government agencies but cannot find support for this program. Mr. Speaker, I chaired the committee which passed the Canada Water Act three years ago, and the Ottawa is one of the river basins that will come under the regulations issued pursuant to that act. The Canada Water Act says that the polluter must pay, but how are you going to make the polluter pay if he went out of business 30, 40 or 50 years ago? This is a new field of operations today. I am using the Ottawa River as an example. I am sure there are many other rivers across the country from which logs could be salvaged and which could form part of a good solid program of conservation. I strongly recommend to the government that this be undertaken, either as a manpower training program or that funds be provided through the Department of the Environment to assist companies like this to clean up waterways and help promote tourism. Many of the outlying areas of Canada are not likely to get steel mills, tire plants or other sophisticated industries.
We have two major industries to offer. One is forest products, which we want to protect, and the other is tourism. We want to make our area as inviting as possible to all the citizens of Canada, the United States, and everywhere else throughout the world. If we are given the money to do the job, we will do it. I strongly plead with the cabinet to provide funds to start this program off either through Manpower, Finance, or the Department of the Environment.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) on his new portfolio and his first budget. I think he deserves credit for the workmanlike way in which he has approached his task. The good news that unemployment declined a bit this month, encouraging though it is, has been off-set by a further increase in prices. And the worst is yet to come. Recent wage settlements have reached new levels and signal even greater price increases in the months ahead.
It is not surprising, therefore, that a recent nation-wide poll aired on the CTV network program "W5" showed inflation as the problem uppermost in people's minds, with unemployment a close second. The country remains in the depths of economic crisis. Is it any wonder, under these circumstances, that there is so much unrest, alienation and a growing trend toward anarchy?
One thing is becoming increasingly clear-four more years of "London School" economics and Canada will split down the middle; Quebec will separate. The social unrest in that province has a largely economic base. There is a very high level of unemployment. Prices are rising. The level of taxation there, as in other parts of Canada, is excessive. Home ownership is becoming a rich man's dream. And wages in many cases, including segments of the public service, are well below $100 a week. People with family responsibilities cannot exist at that rate. The headline in one Montreal newspaper recently underlined the extent of the unrest when it said that Quebec lags in the national economic and employment upswing. It said that notwithstanding the impetus in employment of the last month, Quebec did not share proportionately in even that tiny improvement which took place.
Is it any wonder that there is so much labour unrest? Of course, the present struggle has an ideological tint. Some of the most powerful labour leaders have openly declared their opposition to our private enterprise system. They want to overturn it completely and replace it with their own ill-defined brand of socialism. But they are still a very small minority. The great majority of the workers they represent do not share their philosophy. But in a climate of unemployment, inflation, high taxes and inadequate wages, passions are easily aroused; mob reactions are easy to excite.
To cool the present unrest, some pretty dramatic economic improvement is called for. The federal budget was a small step in the right direction, but totally inadequate to cope with the size of the problem. Tax cuts for manufacturing industry will spur development and assist in
May 23, 1972

offsetting the United States DISC program. Minute adjustments in old age pensions will help but in no way compensate our senior citizens for their substantial loss of purchasing power caused by years of inflation.
On the other hand, the decision to let personal income taxes rise 3 per cent to their former unreasonable levels at the year end is a step backward. Manufacturers are not going to expand their capacity unless ordinary people have enough money, after taxes, to buy the additional output. Instead of an increase in personal income taxes, a further cut for low and medium income earners is urgently required both as an economic stimulus and in the name of justice. Failure to disclose this decision to allow perso-nel income taxes to rise at the end of the year was an error in judgment on the minister's part. It raises question marks in the mind.
Another omission of serious proportions was the government's failure to "come clean" and estimate the likely shortfall in the unemployment insurance fund which will have to be made up as a budgetary item. One local accountant of repute estimated that the shortfall would be between $400 million and $500 million, or even higher. If provision had been made for this estimated shortfall, the anticipated budgetary deficit would be double that announced by the minister; in other words, his estimate could be as much as 100 per cent in error. If this kind of falsification were inflicted on an unsuspecting public by a private corporation, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andras) would cry "Foul" and probably lay charges. Yet the federal government sets the example with impunity.
Most important of all, the budget provided no measures designed to control inflation. The government has gone from one extreme to the other. In 1969-70, inflation was uppermost in their minds and was to be controlled even at the expense of higher unemployment. Now the government says its number one priority is jobs and although lip service paid to the concept of modest price increases, in reality, through its inaction, the government shows that it does not give a hoot about rising prices.
If the government really cared about inflation it would have introduced some form of incomes policy with teeth in it. By one means or another, wages and profits have to be controlled where monopoly power exists. The wage-price spiral must be stopped. Sanity must be restored. The government's abortive voluntary guidelines approach was doomed from the start. A much more realistic approach must be taken if the economy is to be brought under control. Action Canada believes that very simple controls of monopoly power would allow us to pursue the twin goals of full employment and zero inflation. This would be the foundation for an enhanced quality of life.
The classic approach to combines and monopoly power has been anti-combines legislation, but this approach has been almost totally ineffective. The reason, of course, is that oligopolies seldom make formal agreements to set prices. The matter is usually decided around the luncheon table, no records are kept and no evidence exists which would stand up in a court of law. The classic approach has not worked and does not work. And labour unions are not subject to anti-combines legislations at all, so their monopoly power is totally uncontrolled.
The Budget-Mr. Hellyer
There is no alternative to mandatory price and wage guidelines if we are to pursue vigorously and effectively the twin goals of full employment and stable prices at the same time. There are the demands of the consumer. If there is any other solution, I have not heard of it. Monopoly power, no matter what it is called, has to be restrained. Abuse of power by a privileged minority does violence to the principles of a free society.
Someone has referred to the frightening prospects of wage and price controls. A grim picture is painted of a bureaucratic morass similar to that imposed in wartime. Mention was made of ration cards, etc. This comparison of the present situation with that existing in wartime is really quite irresponsible. In wartime there was a physical shortage of goods and services of all kinds. Rationing was essential. In wartime the inflationary pressures were caused by too much money chasing too few goods. It is in these circumstances that black marketeering develops.
Today there is no physical shortage of goods or services of almost any kind, with the possible exception of housing. Today there is an excess of products and not enough money to buy them in the hands of people who need them most. Today rising prices are caused by rising costs. To compare the present situation with the wartime situation is so unbelievably absurd that one wonders why any intelligent person would do so. A red herring of that kind hides the real world and adds nothing to rational debate; it only adds to the depth of confusion.
Wage and price guidelines are not comparable to the bureaucratic controls of wartime. Bureaucrats should not set individual prices. Bureaucrats should not set individual wages. They are not competent to do that; no one knows it better than I do. The kind of price guidelines I suggest would merely limit profits to a certain level of return on capital invested, or in some cases on sales, equal to the long-term experience. Companies would set their own individual prices as they always have in peacetime. Wage increases, where contracts exist, would be limited to the average increase in real output per person in the labour force. Individual wages would be negotiated between management and labour, as they are now, but the total settlement could not exceed the guidelines. In this way union monopoly power would be subject to the public interest and price stability would be possible. Most important of all, this would permit the continuous pursuit of full employment policies.
The pursuit of full employment policies is critically important. The present high level of unemployment is self-destructive and is undermining our society. It has had disastrous consequences for thousands of individual Canadians. I speak with feeling on this matter, Mr. Speaker, because the people of my riding, Trinity, are directly affected. They are people with incomes below the national average. They are people who work with their hands. They work in construction and in factories; they are needle workers and office workers. They are people who are directly and immediately affected by any downturn in our economy. Many of them have lost their jobs and their capital goods as a result. Many of them have cashed in their insurance policies and used the proceeds to meet current requirements. I know of one family which had to give up a house after having made mortgage payments for

May 23, 1972
The Budget-Mr. Hellyer
20 years. It is this kind of distress which cannot be taken lightly. It might be different if it were necessary, but in a country like Canada it is completely unnecessary and for that reason some of us feel impelled to speak out loudly on behalf of these people.
Reducing the present totally unacceptable level of 6 per cent unemployment to, let us say, 3 per cent, which would merely represent those persons changing jobs, would require a fantastic increase in capital investment. At the rate of $25,000 capital investment per person it would require an additional $7.5 billion to provide jobs for 300,000 people. When I use the figure of $25,000 capital investment per person, I am reminded by my economist friends that that figure is much too low; they suggest a more realistic figure would be $50,000 per person. If one is to use the figure of $50,000 per person, the amount required would be $15 billion.
The government has failed to realize the magnitude of the job. Its relief to industry will help provide jobs for new people entering the labour force, but no provision has been made for the investment required to do more than nibble at the backlog. That fact has been underlined by the figures I have quoted. The backlog of capital investment required in order to bring unemployment down from 6 per cent to about half that figure, which might be considered satisfactory in this country, would be somewhere between $7.5 billion and $15 billion over and above that which normally would be required to provide for new entrants to the labour force.
It is perfectly obvious that if the Canadian economy is to survive and prosper, monopoly power must be effectively curbed in the public interest. The size of the political vacuum in Canada today can be measured by the fact that none of the existing parties is willing to undertake this difficult, thankless but essential task. If Action Canada's policy is put into effect, we will then be in a position to solve a whole series of related problems.
At the present time we are underproducing by $3 billion to $5 billion dollars a year in real terms. This is due to the unemployment of men and underemployment of machines. If we went to the full employment solution we would have an extra $3 billion to $5 billion of resources annually, over and above normal growth, to use for the elimination of poverty, the elimination of slums, the construction of urban transportation systems, the provision of adequate housing, the control of pollution and the development of Canadian industries and resources by Canadians. That is a tremendous amount of resources and would finance many homes at $25,000 each, the rehabilitation of many old houses at $5,000 to $6,000, the construction of sewage disposal systems, of garbage recycling systems, the supplementing of incomes at the low end of the scale and for more adequate supplements for old age pensioners, and the provision of meaningful employment for young people.
In summation, the government has failed to level with the Canadian people. The government has failed to take steps adequate to cope with the present level of unemployment. It has done nothing to relieve the tax burden on the lower and middle income groups. It has provided inade-

quate relief for our senior citizens and, finally, the government has stubbornly refused to take the action necessary to curb the abuse of monopoly power by big unions and big business in order to restore price stability and protect the weak and unorganized. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, the government deserves the censure of this House.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because the first part of this budget, old age security, the guaranteed supplement legislation and the war veterans pension legislation has already been debated, there is no need to discuss these problems further except to say that the government has moved from its position of making the old age pension static at $85 back to some degree of universality for all Canadians regardless of their economic status. The move of the government a year ago to freeze the old age pension at $80 and gradually phase it out and relate it to the income of the individual has been thwarted, at least for the time being.
I now come to what the budget is doing for business and the economy of the country, that segment which sustains the welfare of Canadians. In this respect the government has been woefully inadequate. Its moves will not help this country to surmount its problems in unemployment and its relations with the outside world, particularly the United States. The stepping down of Mr. Connally, the tough-minded individual who made a start on realigning the policy of the United States both financial and trade, indicates that we are at the end of an era. The regime of Mr. Connally indicates that as a dominant western nation the United States has had to make moves in the interest of that country to strengthen and turn around the balance of payments of the American economy.
The United States has served notice that we cannot expect further favoured nation agreements with the inauguration of the inquiry into Michelin tire exports, the alleged dumping of aluminum into the United States, the controversy over the Canada-United States auto pact and its implication that we are getting the best deal. They have served notice that our manufactured goods are facing increased surveillance protectionism in the United States market.
Similarly, the strong American protectionist sentiment established the union espousal of the Burke-Hartke law in the United States with their proposal that the present American economic structure exports jobs from the United States. We can make no mistake about that. This refers to the export of jobs to Canada in branch plants, and so on, and the American unions have indicated their support for any move to prevent this.
What are the main problems facing Canadians in the immediate future? It is quite obvious that unemployment is of vital and immediate concern. Consequently, what will be our industrial and commercial strategy to provide jobs on a strong growth basis for the years ahead? The unemployment level is far too high, with over 600,000 persons being classified as unemployed. However, much of this unemployment can be ascribed to the high birth rate of the fifties. With a drop from the birth rate of the fifties and indications of a continuing drop, we are now witnessing a drop in the labour force. This will become
May 23, 1972

progressive and in another five years or so there should be no need to create jobs in large amounts.
The jobs needed should be generated by a modest growth of the economy. The government's strategy of tax cuts to manufacturing and processing firms will not be of much value. I object to treating various sectors of the economy in a wildly different fashion. That is what this cut for manufacturing and processing does. There is a strong case for leaving the allocation of resources to the normal competitive processes of the market rather than using crude and non-reliable tax concessions. These introduce a new sense of distortion into the functioning of the marketing system and substitute therefor the judgment of the Minister of Finance as to what types of tax relief make for growth in our competitive system.
This policy will create more disparities in the various regions of the country and will benefit areas which are now considered largely aggressive. It does not do anything for the western grain industry which exports well over 10 per cent of our total export earnings into world markets other than the United States. This tax concession to manufacturers and processors will not in any way help the agricultural industry. I cannot even see where meat processing plants will benefit. There is no obvious reason why the manufacturing sector of our economy should be favoured. It is a myth that only the manufacturing sector creates jobs. Studies have shown that most of our manufacturers have to find a market in the United States and, seemingly, this area will be increasingly closed in the immediate future.
If the government is interested in creating jobs, it is going about it in the wrong way. All economics show overwhelmingly that the service area is the biggest producer of jobs in an immediate way. If it is necessary to counteract the DISC program, it would have been more appropriate to have a similar plan in Canada to encourage exports. The cut in corporation tax for manufacturing and processing firms will benefit companies which receive high profits in the short-run and will do nothing for companies that are getting started or are not in a profitable position. Indeed, it is estimated that substantial savings will end up in the United States treasury due to the fact that many profitable manufacturing firms are American owned.
Erratic variations in tax rates do little, even if they are favourable or result in a lower tax rate. A budget was brought down in June, 1971. This was followed by the 7 per cent temporary tax reduction last October. The tax reform legislation passed last December attempted to set out tax schedules for the ensuing three years. Now we have another haphazard change with the 9 per cent tax cut for manufacturers and processors.
Then there is the added uncertainty of defining what is manufacturing and processing and what is not. It could be months before these will be defined by the tax department. This makes it impossible to plan ahead intelligently. Large industrial organizations need to plan at least three years in advance, so long-term plans must be passed upon something more than the whim of the Minister of Finance. Frequent changes in tax rates are counterproductive. All
The Budget-Mr. Ritchie
people recognize that uncertainty about expectations inhibits investment. Businessmen do not know what to do because they cannot anticipate which parts of the economy will be supported or what will be the duration of the assistance.
Mr. Speaker, the budget implies that investment can better be stimulated by tax reductions to corporations than by across the board tax cuts. Our main deficiency today is still consumer demand; only when consumption catches up with investment in a significant range of industries will more stimulus be needed. The tax reductions for corporations will call forth little additions in investment. There is still plenty of unused plant utilization available for expansion.
At the same time, personal income taxes are going up as a result of the expiration of the temporary tax reduction. Over the past 20 years the Canadian government has become increasingly dependent on personal income tax as a source of revenue. The increase in direct taxes upon individuals over the past 15 years is almost twice as great as the increase in direct taxes upon corporations during the same period. An across the board tax cut in income tax at least for those below the $20,000 bracket would have the effect of increasing consumer demand, which we need immediately, and of contributing to savings, the ultimate source of investment and growth.
There is one area in which the Minister of Finance can quickly and easily increase economic growth and provide immediate jobs. He can clarify the investment provisions as they affect small companies in the sphere of ineligible investment income. An analysis of the affairs of small companies is showing that the relevant provision in the tax bill just passed is having a most damaging effect on the formation of new, small companies created by the investment and savings of other small companies. In its attempt to close the loophole of using the small company as a tax avoidance area, the government has drastically slowed up enterprise in this area. New, small companies quickly create jobs as compared to larger companies which require a longer period of planning. They are particularly important to areas of this country away from the large cities where pools of capital have been concentrated.
The accelerated write-off and the provisions of the budget expanding capital cost allowances for machinery are a simple recognition that taxation policies have been changed to respond to corporate wishes. This type of program will be utilized as a gimmick by many companies to derive maximum tax benefits. These changes will not have much impact on our high unemployment rate because they cannot be implemented by many corporations on short notice. These capital cost allowances permit the deferment of taxes which could result in increasing the cash flow. In subsequent years these same corporations will have written off many of their assets and therefore could be short of funds to pay their taxes. This happened in the late 1960s following the previous period of accelerated depreciation.
Constantly introducing tax changes will have only a temporary effect on our economy. Our economic difficulties have their origin in the Benson, Basford and Bryce proposal which flocked out of Ottawa and have been aggravated by the level of the Canadian dollar which is in
2482

May 23, 1972
The Budget-Mr. Ritchie
turn the result of improper fiscal and monetary policies. It appears the Liberals have been converted to Social Credit theory in vain efforts to bring down the exchange value of the Canadian dollar. There have been astounding increases in the money supply.
Over the last two years the annual increase has been close to 18 per cent. Increases in money supply of this magnitude have fueled inflation but have had little apparent effect on the Canadian dollar which continues to creep higher. Also, over the past two months the Bank of Canada has used more than $200 million to buy U.S. dollars and thereby restrain the level of the Canadian dollar. Certainly $200 million could be more advantageously spent.
What is needed now is gradual, expanded stimulus; in other words, lower taxes in all categories. Good fiscal policy should be implemented to effect real demand in all sectors of the economy, including exports. The Trudeau cabinet continues to try to substitute its adjustments for those of the marketplace.
Elaborate variations in the treatment of a particular segment of the economy, the manufacturing and processing group, illustrate the administration's bias but little else. Frequent shifts in taxation rates, four changes within one year, create so much uncertainty that investment decisions will not be made. Tax cuts for corporations ignore the common sense view that investment is not going to increase while excess capacity abounds. The shift and emphasis to give more weight to personal income tax was illustrated by the effective increase in personal income taxes which will become payable next year and, as well, corporations which do not fall into the manufacturing category will find their rates go up by 7 J per cent on the first of next year.
The economy is suffering from too much pushing and prodding. Broad tax cuts would bring down the external value of the Canadian dollar and we could be sure that savings eventually would be channelled into spending and investment, perhaps even into plant expansion if necessary. If secondary manufacturing needs help, surely it could be provided in much better ways. Encouragement of export activities is one area in which government could do something. Trade bloc agreements would be of great benefit to the Canadian export industry. We should allow our economy to function and do the things that it does best.
The preferred treatment to manufacturing given by this budget would seem to indicate that the government is embarking upon a so-called industrial policy on the basis that manufacturing is the area which needs help. There is serious doubt in the minds of many people that manufacturing will provide the entry into world markets which Canada's industrial machine is seeking. In a report of the Science Council of Canada published in October, 1971, and entitled "Innovation of a Cold Climate", there are some very interesting statistics. They show that between 1961 and 1967 manufacturing employment increased by 25 per cent. In 1968 this growth faltered and has remained static since. This is not because of lack of technologists because Canada has been graduating these people by the thousand.
The decline in this area has been in part brought about by technology itself being able to supply the same volume of goods with fewer employees. It is significant that in Canada it is precisely those industries from which most was expected in employment, tax revenue and consumer benefits which are now in difficulty.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock I was quoting some statements made by the Science Council of Canada on the difficulties that manufacturing is now experiencing in Canada. They said it is significant that in Canada it is precisely those industries from which most was to be expected by way of employment, tax revenue and consumer benefits that are now in difficulty. No new manufacturing industries are in sight, and low technology industries simply cannot shoulder alone the responsibility of meeting our expectations of a better standard of living. The adoption of appropriate over-all monetary and fiscal policies will take the country back toward a satisfactory rate of economic growth. What is needed is to eliminate the elements in the tax system which inhibit growth and promote inefficiency.
The budget takes no cognizance of the increasing change in the approach of youth to the work ethic. Youth is questioning the goals and values of education and the effort involved is seeking a diploma. We have always had this, but it is on the increase in today's society. An increasing number of student dropouts are coming from all sections of the economy and a growing number of young people are opting for non-employment. It is becoming increasingly feasible to live on part-time wages, a situation fostered by a relatively affluent welfare system and an unemployment insurance scheme which in effect is a modification of a guaranteed income.
It seems likely that a growing number of tomorrow's employees will not have the same ideas and aspirations of those of today. Economic, social and political structures will have to be prepared to accommodate these changing attitudes in planning modifications to job content. It is to be kept in mind that employment is becoming increasingly concentrated in the service sector. All this indicates that society is questioning traditional values. The failure of the budget to continue the service aspect of our society must be looked upon as one of the detrimental features of this budget.
I wish to turn for a moment to the foreign investment proposals put forward by the government. In Canada's case, foreign investment is synonymous with United States investment which is the investment we fear. It seems ironic that at this time the aims of the DISC program in the United States, which is causing such consternation in Canada, are the same as those of the proposed foreign takeover committee proposed by the cabinet. Both are designed to keep United States investment at home, and this will provide jobs for Americans.

May 23, 1972

If United States investment can be an instrument of domination, it is also the principal vehicle of technological change. It introduces manufacturing processes as well as new management techniques. It forces our manufacturers to rationalize and modernize, something they would not accept without competition. If we continue to permit outside investments or takeover, we will share in the profits that foreign investors make. Obviously these profits, spread throughout the economy, raise the general standard of living.
We could curtail takeovers by foreign companies, but they would merely establish or enlarge branch plants here with adverse effects on domestic companies. If we turn foreign investment away, these funds will go to other countries. On the other hand, foreign investment does impose limitations on national development in addition to the limitations inherent in the whole process of industrial activity.
For those of us in western Canada, the keeping out of foreign investment would mean replacement by eastern financial interests because of the need in western Canada for investment capital. The possibility of legislating against foreign investment, just as our present efforts to control it, would be negated because eastern capital would be in a position to force Ottawa to impose conditions in its own interests. The best thing to do about foreign investment is concentrate on everything possible to encourage industrial dynamism which will attract the entrepreneur of our society. Experience shows that the entrepreneur of new processes has a greater advantage over his rival and innovation is the major source of profit. We need to attract this talent.
The portion of this budget which deals with the economy of the nation is not conducive to steady and sustained growth. It will not provide jobs immediately, nor will it make provision for future years when our job needs will be less.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. Olson (Minister of Agriculture):

With inflationary dollars.

speechtext: The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) is now doing something I intend to deal with in greater depth in a few moments, that is, he is deliberately attempting to depreciate and downgrade the performance of Canadians in developing our economy by setting out distortions as to what is actually happening to the point that we do not as Canadians take as much satisfaction as we should.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
I have two main reasons for entering the debate this evening, the first of which is to set out in clear, concise and accurate terms the record of the performance of the agricultural sector of the Canadian economy during 1971 as opposed to not only the immediate preceding year but the previous ten-year period. My second reason is to refute this kind of distortion to which the opposition must resort when it does not have any better arguments.
I should also like to refer to misinterpretations and misrepresentations that have been made by some otherwise responsible members of the opposition when dealing with provisions in the budget which they claim to be discriminatory of agricultural production in so far as processing and manufacturing is concerned. Opposition members have had some success in this regard from time to time, in that they have fooled the public for a while with these distorted interpretations to the point that some sincere and well meaning citizens believe them. Therefore, I think it appropriate that we scotch these misrepresentations and misinterpretations early rather than assume that everyone will dismiss them for the kind of allegation they are.
Let us consider some of these misrepresentations. There are one or two other things I should say. Some of my colleagues from western Canada are now travelling about the country suggesting there is nothing in the budget of significance for western Canada. They repeat this to the point that they believe it themselves. It seems to me that the leaders of the governments of the prairie provinces, whether they be Social Credit, Conservative or NDP, have been going around the country attempting to attract manufacturing and processing industries to establish within their provinces. There is no more attractive way to do that than by developing a sustainable basis of the kind the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) outlined in the budget in relation to corporation tax cuts.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, be serious.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As I suggest, every person in the four western provinces has talked himself into believing that the most important economic thrust we can make in this area is in attracting additional secondary manufacturing, including processing, to establish there. We have always agreed that the first stage in development should take place in primary industry such as agriculture, mining and oil and gas development. We have reached the second stage. We ought now to be encouraging secondary manufacturing, including processing, to establish and expand. It is in this general area that we find a higher labour input by Canadians.
It is fair to say that in the oil and gas industry, for example, exploration, development and injecting addi-

tional and larger volumes into the market stream will provide an impetus to our economy. I am sure this will continue. The petrochemical industry has only just begun operations in western Canada. I am sure it will gain a tremendous advantage from the cuts in corporation taxes which were made for this purpose. The accelerated rate of write-offs, up to 50 per cent, of the cost of new equipment going into this industry will be of tremendous advantage to western Canada.

I have mentioned only a few industries which will benefit. We must remember the tar sands development in Alberta which has really only just started. We can envisage markets looming in the future of tremendous volume and range for the development of this resource. Certainly the provision in respect of depreciation of processing equipment, as well as the new tax structure, will be of tremendous advantage in this area. Hon. members from western Canada should look at the facts and give Canadians the hope and optimism justifiable as a result of this budget, particularly in the secondary manufacturing area which we all agree is the area in which we as a nation should be moving.
I should like to return briefly to the suggestion that there has been some kind of discrimination in this budget against manufacturers and processors who use agricultural raw products. speechtext: Who are they?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It would be easy to mention their names. They do not spend enough time in this House, so they are not here tonight. But the record is clear. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will this apply in respect of all products?

The hon. member is doing exactly what he did in committee; he is asking the Minister of Agriculture to give a legal interpretation of the application of the law which quite properly comes under the Department of National Revenue. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know they would have a great deal of difficulty in the farm area because of this garbage they have been peddling for the past two or three years. Farmers now know how productive the government's policies have been for their purposes. When we assumed office in 1968, so far as agriculture was concerned we made clear that the major thrust of the Department of Agriculture, and indeed of the government as a whole, in the agricultural field would be to turn the emphasis toward the marketing aspect of agricultural products because we believed the greatest enchancement of benefits for farmers would be available from emphasis in that area. I suggest that for years the Department of Agriculture has done an excellent job under all governments in those areas in which it has been active.
I suggest there are two main areas involved. One is in the resolution of production problems through such means as the research stations we have across the country, the health of animals branch, and so on. In other words, advance in production technology was one of the main functions. The department did this very well; in fact, it did it so well in many cases that the capacity to produce has far outstripped the advancement in marketing and marketing technology.
The second main area in which the Department of Agriculture has been involved is perhaps one which could be broadly described as the regulatory function. Making inspections and grading agricultural products such as vegetables, poultry, beef and so on in order to make sure that while these products went through the merchandising and distribution system the grades were maintained both on behalf of the producer who was selling and the consumer who was buying the product. As I have said, we made a deliberate announcement that the emphasis would be on the marketing sector for the purpose of improving the position of the primary producer in respect of market-
May 23, 1972

ing functions and structures. We have followed that policy consistently since that time.
We might look at the result of having done this for nearly four years in order to see what the rate of success has been. For example, Canadian farmers on the average in 1971 came through a much improved year. The average gross income per farm-by the way, this is something members of the opposition never talk about-rose to an all-time high of $13,589 in 1971 compared to $10,678 the year before. In other words, it is up almost 25 per cent. That just lays the basis. The average net income also rose in 1971 to $3,946 from $3,160 the year before. This is something I am sure members of the opposition will never repeat outside this House. That is an improvement of 23.6 per cent in just one year. That is pretty important, but it is even more important to point out that taken over a ten-year period the improvement is 70.3 per cent.
Hon. members like to hold up years like 1966, for example, and say that everything has gone down according to that one particular year. The Liberal party was in office in 1966 and does not want to take anything away from that great year. It was a great year for agriculture. No one denies that. We sold the largest amount of wheat, at the highest price, in Canadian history. There is no doubt about that. Hon. members, however, like to make comparisons between 1966 only and 1971. They do not want to make comparisons between 1971 and the ten-year average. All they want to do is make comparisons between that year and the highest peak, the year of the great surge in grain sales under a Liberal government.
I would like also to draw attention to the fact that total grain receipts in 1971 were up by $120 million over the year before. If hon. members would like me to spell out in detail the figures for oilseed, for barley, for oats and for wheat I would be happy to do that, but I can tell them that there were increases in every single grain commodity.

prices-this varies somewhat from province to province because it is the province which sets the amount of payment to the producers-and the change in the holdback by the price changes that we took in 1971 and the improved market conditions, for which we take credit, amount to somewhere between 85 cents and $1 per hundred for the producers.
