speakeroldname: Mr. Ray Perrault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-DELAY IN PAYMENT OF BENEFITS-ACTION TO PREVENT LOANSHARK OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to answer the question the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Rowland) asked during the question period on May 8. I listened with interest to his observations this evening. I assure him, again, that the minister and the department are considering actively the problem he spoke about again this evening.
By order in council PC 1972-667 an amendment to the unemployment insurance regulations was made which reads as follows:
Section 145 of the unemployment insurance regulations is amended by adding thereto the following subsection (8);
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
A claimant making a claim for benefit shall, unless otherwise permitted by the commission, supply the mailing address of his normal place of residence.
This, the hon. member will observe, will prevent claimants from advising the Unemployment Insurance Commission of a change of address which could be that of a lender. Most hon. members know that loansharks oblige people about to receive benefits to have them mailed to their civic address, to ensure that they get back the moneys lent plus the extravagant interest rate for which they are asking.
In addition to this amendment to the unemployment insurance regulations, investigations of which the hon. member is aware have proceeded for some weeks. These investigations may lead to additional measures to protect the interests of the unemployed of this country. Indeed, active consideration is being given to possible actions. I hope it may be possible to make further announcements later.
One of the findings that has emerged from the investigations is that there is not necessarily a relationship between delays in unemployment insurance benefits, for whatever reason-those mistakes might be on the part of the claimant or the commission or anyone else-and the so-called loansharking operation. Indeed, loansharking began long before changes were made in the unemployment insurance regulations of this country. Nevertheless, that practice is deplored by the minister, by the department and certainly by the government. Any useful suggestions received from any part of the House will be welcome and will be given careful and attentive study by the minister, to make sure we can end this practice.

maintopic: HUMAN SCIENCES-PROGRAMS TO INCREASE PUBLIC EXPENDITURE
HUMAN SCIENCES-PROGRAMS TO INCREASE PUBLIC EXPENDITURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 17 I asked the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) to take note of statistics which had just come to my attention from Statistics Canada indicating that the government of this country spends 15 times more on the natural than on the human sciences. I asked if the government was so totally committed to technological efforts that it was not contemplating further expenditures on the human sciences.
From my university background I have noted over many years that the relationship between the human sciences and the engineering and natural sciences is something like that of Lazarus to Dives, but I was appalled and disturbed that the gap had widened between these two with the assistance of government. The document which stimulated my concern is entitled "Federal government expenditures on the human sciences," catalogue 13-545, published by Statistics Canada. One quotation is startling. It reads as follows:
The expenditures on activities in the human sciences are rather modest when compared to the expenditures for the engineering and natural sciences. For instance, the current expenditures on R & D in the human sciences represent only 7 per cent of the equivalent in the natural sciences in 1969-70. Moreover, this proportion drops to 6 per cent if capital expenditures (important in

May 23, 1972
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion the natural sciences but almost non-existent in the human sciences) are included in the calculation.
Comparison of total expenditures on scientific activities for these two areas shows that for one dollar spent in the human sciences in 1969-70, there was a corresponding expenditure of almost eight dollars in the engineering and natural sciences. However, forecasted expenditures for 1970-71 and 1971-72 indicate a small 'improvement', which expected ratios of $l/$7 for these two years (excluding the census costs).
This matter is one of great concern, especially at a time when there is renewed concern in Canada about such questions as our national identity, cultural heritage, and so on; when we find that there is a seeming drying up of expenditure on the part of the government on those things which one might say expresses the Canadian soul. Not long ago I saw a very moving editorial in the Ottawa Citizen entitled "Canada Council beheaded," written by Christopher Young. He wrote:
The government acted with commendable speed in filling the vacancy at the top of the CBC. Only performance will tell whether vice-president Laurent Picard is the right choice to run the national broadcasting network, but at least there will be no hiatus at the top. Mr. Picard was appointed three months before the resignation of George Davidson was to take effect.
This is a great difference from the situation with regard to the Canada Council. I again quote:
The council's director, Peter Dwyer, suffered a severe stroke while at work a year ago. Mr. Dwyer had worked in the Privy Council under the St. Laurent government and had drafted the act setting up the Canada Council, on the basis of recommendations made by the Massey commission. He had moved to the council's staff when it was founded in 1957 and had directed its highly successful arts program from the beginning.
It was apparent rather quickly that Mr. Dwyer would not be able to return to the heavy administrative job at the head of the council's permanent staff. His formal resignation was announced last November, and he is now a consultant to the National Arts Centre.
But nothing has been done to fill the post, and the council is drifting aimlessly. Decisions are deferred. New ideas are discouraged. Staff morale is wretched. The council itself, made up of distinguished or politically acceptable citizens, has failed to fill the vacuum of leadership.
The public servants who work at the council and the people in the arts who have come to depend on its advice and funds-at least those I have spoken to-are appalled by the effects of the government's failure to act. Whether indifference or indecision is the reason, the results are serious-
Meantime some of the newer government agencies-notably the Local Initiatives Program and Opportunities for Youth-are moving into areas where a more dynamic Canada Council might be expected to be active-
The Canada Council does not loom as large in the national consciousness as the CBC. But its importance to the writers, musicians, painters, actors and dancers, as well as the university professors, of this country can hardly be exaggerated-
Governments need to be checked not only on those things which they ought to have done but also on not doing those things which they ought to have done.
This sounds very episcopalian.
The government-and specifically the prime minister whose prerogative this appointment is-ought to have acted on the Canada Council vacancy long before now.
I think that these two things unite in a most disturbing way the heavy expenditure on the natural sciences and engineering and the very miniscule expenditure on the tremendously important realm of the human sciences. The fact that the Canada Council leadership seems not to

have commanded any priority causes me a great deal of anxiety. I say this as one who believes that while the natural sciences are important, while the structure of Canada, its basic engineering, is important, surely the soul of Canada is still more important even than these and this priority should be reflected by a sensitive and thoughtful government.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ray Perrault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
maintopic: HUMAN SCIENCES-PROGRAMS TO INCREASE PUBLIC EXPENDITURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's question follows a report issued by Statistics Canada outlining the discrepancy in government spending between technical sciences and human sciences. Although we must acknowledge the existence of such a discrepancy, let us put it into proper perspective.
It seems that the figures provided did not include the Department of the Secretary of State, the Public Archives, the CRTC, the National Library, the Company of Young Canadians, the National Film Board, the Canadian Film Development Corporation, the National Arts Centre, the CBC or the Opportunities for Youth program, to mention but a few. All these programs are closely related to human sciences, since they deal with people, and the bulk of their expenditures is directed toward aspects of Canadian life that are of a humanistic nature.
I am aware that the hon. member is thinking in terms of moneys distributed to provide assistance to specific research in sociology, political science and anthropology, but I am sure he will agree that a good many of the reports and studies paid for by the federal government, or its agencies, whether it be the youth report or whatever, fit very well into those criteria. Furthermore, the people employed to carry out those taks are mainly social scientists.
I would like to terminate my remarks by saying that the distinction made by confining human research to technological research is somewhat rhetorical. It can be argued that a botanist, a chemist, an environmental specialist deals as much with the well-being of people as does a sociologist. The federal government is attempting to infuse this concept in its apparatus and in this respect is studying very closely the recommendations of the report of the Senate Special Committee on Science Policy. That particular report has stressed this aspect of sciences and has offered most valuable comments.

maintopic: GRAIN-PILOT PROJECT FOR USE OF INTERIOR ELEVATORS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT
GRAIN-PILOT PROJECT FOR USE OF INTERIOR ELEVATORS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the last several years since the introduction of the task force report on agriculture in 1969-70 there has been considerable discussion concerning the use of inland terminals and unit trains. The minister in charge of the Wheat Board told us last winter that very soon a report on transportation arrangements in the Dominion of Canada will be tabled in the House of Commons. Yet we sit here today, soon to be in the month of June, and no report is forthcoming.
In lieu of an announcement by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) in Winnipeg concerning the movement of
May 23, 1972

grain through inland terminals for cleaning and shipment, I asked the Minister of Agriculture the following question:
Since the federal government is going ahead with a pilot project to determine the feasibility of channelling grain through large interior terminal elevators, I wonder if the minister would be prepared to make a statement on motions outlining some of the details of this program, such as the elevator companies involved and so on.
I asked the question because of the many implications of this project for the Prairies generally in terms of the use of inland terminals. I inquired whether the government had established objectives, whether it had estimated the cost of operating the necessary trucks, whether it had decided who should lease the trucks and how the private elevator companies would be involved. How would the grain be cleaned and shipped out? This information should be laid on the table without delay so that interested parties in the prairie region can form an opinion as to the government's objectives and the significance of the program by comparison to the expected end results-results which should also be publicly stated.
I make this suggestion no matter on what side of the debate on the use of inland terminals a group may happen to be. These groups, whether the Palliser Wheat Growers Association, the National Farmers Union, the wheat pools, the Pioneer Elevator Company, or what have you, should have the opportunity to know exactly what is going on in terms of the use of inland terminals and to understand the implications for our transportation system. Ministers speak of moving so much grain to the west coast, but at the same time I suggest we cannot ignore the problems that we faced during last winter. We must look at different methods of grain movement and grain handling in terms of one principle above all others, and that is service to the farmers involved. There is no use completely changing the system if this merely adds up to
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
additional cost of production for farmers whose prices for grain commodities are already far too low.
All kinds of ideas are being put forward in this country, indeed in the world, regarding grain movement. The United States has been developing the use of water transportation facilities, different types of barges to haul goods, especially farm products. Some of the railroad companies, such as Pullman in the United States, have developed certain ideas that are based on the use of container cars and larger door openings in grain cars to facilitate quicker loading of grain. There are all kinds of methods that the government can examine. But the most significant and important aspect of this kind of project is that there be complete consultation with those directly involved who will be directly affected after the program has been implemented.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Lessard (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: GRAIN-PILOT PROJECT FOR USE OF INTERIOR ELEVATORS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to the hon. member's request for details on a pilot project to channel grains through interior terminal elevators, I might say simply that this project is for feed barley only. This barley will be trucked from various private country elevators under instruction from the Canadian Wheat Board to the Canadian government elevators at Moose Jaw and Saskatoon. At this point it will be cleaned, segregated by grade and made ready for reshipment pending instructions from the Wheat Board. At the end of this crop year the pilot project will end and an evaluation will be made. I might point out, Mr. Speaker, that the project will be useful not only for purposes of evaluation but it is expected that four million bushels of barley will be put through the system under the project.
The hon. member also raised other points. However, I can only say that this experiment was undertaken on the recommendation of those who were greatly involved in grain transportation in this country.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.25 p.m.

Wednesday. May 24, 1972
